makes.name: Alfa Romeo
makes.overview: The passionate Italian driver's marque, renowned in Australia for melodic twin-cam engines, Bathurst class victories, and the Giorgio-platform Giulia and Stelvio.

makes.name: Alpine
makes.overview: Dieppe's legendary lightweight French sports car marque, selling the exquisite mid-engine A110 in Australia through bespoke Alpine centres.

makes.name: Aston Martin
makes.overview: Handcrafted British high-performance grand tourers, combining timeless elegance with muscular V8 and V12 symphonies in Australia.

makes.name: Audi
makes.overview: Audi represents Vorsprung durch Technik in Australia, celebrated for quattro all-wheel drive, RS performance estates, and high-tech luxury SUVs.

makes.name: Austin / Morris (BMC Australia)
makes.overview: The British Motor Corporation's Australian manufacturing titan at Victoria Park / Zetland Sydney, producing millions of Morris Minors, Austin Cambridges, Austin 1800s, and unique Australian six-cylinder Kimberley and Tasman models.

makes.name: BMW
makes.overview: The Ultimate Driving Machine in Australia, renowned for sports sedans, touring car dominance at Mount Panorama, and pioneering luxury X-series SUVs.

makes.name: BYD
makes.overview: Build Your Dreams has rapidly evolved into Australia's second-biggest electric vehicle brand, celebrated for ultra-safe Blade Battery tech, the Atto 3, Seal sports sedan, and the groundbreaking Shark 6 plug-in hybrid ute.

makes.name: Bentley
makes.overview: Crewe's master of peerless grand touring luxury and effortless torque, celebrated in Australia for W12 and V8 Continental GTs and Bentayga luxury SUVs.

makes.name: Bolwell
makes.overview: Bolwell Cars was founded in Melbourne, Victoria in 1962 by brothers Graeme and Campbell Bolwell. Bolwell is Australia's most enduring and respected bespoke sports car manufacturer. Beginning with fiberglass kit sports cars (Mk IV and Mk VII), Bolwell achieved international acclaim in 1970 with the Nagari (Mk VIII), a fully productionized road-legal supercar featuring a steel backbone chassis, fiberglass body, and Ford 302ci/351ci V8 power. In the 21st century, Bolwell leveraged advanced aerospace vacuum-infused carbon composites to produce the Nagari 300 and Nagari 500 mid-engine supercars.

makes.name: Brabham Automotive
makes.overview: Brabham Automotive was established in 2018 in Adelaide, South Australia by David Brabham (son of triple Formula One World Champion Sir Jack Brabham) in partnership with Australian advanced manufacturing company Fusion Capital. Operating from a state-of-the-art facility in Edinburgh Parks, Adelaide, Brabham set out to build an uncompromised track and road hypercar: the Brabham BT62. Weighing just 972 kg dry, the BT62 featured a carbon-fibre composite monocoque chassis, advanced aerodynamics generating over 1,200 kg of downforce, carbon-carbon brakes, and a mid-mounted naturally aspirated 5.4-litre modular V8 generating 522 kW (700 hp) and 667 Nm, revving to 8,200 rpm through a 6-speed Holinger sequential paddle-shift racing gearbox. In 2020, Brabham introduced the road-compliant BT62R. The vehicle achieved lap records at Mount Panorama and Adelaide Motorsport Festival before operations concluded in 2024.

makes.name: Buckle / Goggomobil Australia
makes.overview: Buckle Motors was founded by Sydney automotive entrepreneur and racing driver Bill Buckle. To bypass steep Australian import tariffs on completed motor vehicles in the late 1950s, Buckle negotiated with Hans Glas GmbH in Germany to import rolling chassis of the Goggomobil microcar, manufacturing fiberglass sedan, coupe, and van bodies at his Punchbowl and Brookvale workshops in Sydney. In 1959, Buckle designed and released his masterpiece: the Goggomobil Dart. A doorless, two-seat aerodynamic roadster weighing only 345 kg and standing just 1.1 meters tall, the Dart was powered by a rear-mounted 300cc or 400cc air-cooled twin-cylinder two-stroke engine. The Dart achieved lasting Australian fame, becoming a beloved cultural icon celebrated for its delightful styling and timeless Yellow Pages television commercials.

makes.name: Cadillac
makes.overview: General Motors' flagship luxury brand, officially entering Australia in 2024 as an all-electric prestige brand led by the Lyriq SUV.

makes.name: Caterham
makes.overview: The pure evolution of Colin Chapman's Lotus Seven, delivering peerless power-to-weight track performance and road legality in Australia.

makes.name: Chery
makes.overview: Pioneered early low-cost imports (J1 and J11) via Ateco in 2011, before relaunching in 2023 as a direct factory brand with the stylish Omoda 5 and Tiggo SUV families.

makes.name: Chevrolet / GMSV
makes.overview: Historically assembled by General Motors-Holden across four decades, and reborn through GM Specialty Vehicles (GMSV) with Clayton-remanufactured Silverado trucks and factory RHD Corvette C8.

makes.name: Chrysler / Valiant Australia
makes.overview: Chrysler Australia Ltd was established in June 1951 following Chrysler Corporation's acquisition of Adelaide coachbuilder Richards Industries. Operating from its monumental manufacturing complex at Tonsley Park and engine foundry at Lonsdale in South Australia, Chrysler was the third of the 'Big Three' Australian domestic automakers alongside Holden and Ford. In January 1962, Chrysler launched the revolutionary Valiant (R-Series), whose 145 hp Slant-6 engine instantly out-accelerated and outperformed every rival on Australian roads. In 1970, Chrysler Australia's local engineering team created the iconic HEMI-6 engine, featuring hemispherical combustion chambers and producing massive torque. The following year, Chrysler introduced the VH Valiant Charger—backed by the unforgettable 'Hey Charger!' advertising campaign—whose triple-Weber E49 'Six Pack' became the fastest-accelerating Australian production car for over a decade. Facing financial distress in the late 1970s, Chrysler Australia sold its operations to Mitsubishi Motors Corporation in 1980, creating Mitsubishi Motors Australia Limited (MMAL). The Chrysler brand was later re-introduced as an American import arm (300C, PT Cruiser, Voyager) before departing Australia in 2021.

makes.name: Citroën
makes.overview: The avant-garde French innovator that gave Australia local assembly of the ID19/DS19, hydraulic magic-carpet ride comfort, and historic rally victories.

makes.name: Cupra
makes.overview: SEAT's performance-oriented, design-led Spanish brand, launching Australia as its very first market expansion outside Europe in 2022.

makes.name: Daewoo
makes.overview: Popular 1990s and early-2000s Korean value brand in Australia, known for 'Free Care' 3-year servicing before its models were absorbed into Holden.

makes.name: Daihatsu
makes.overview: Pioneers of compact 3-cylinder economy cars and nimble mini-4x4s, beloved for the Charade, Rocky, and Feroza.

makes.name: Deepal
makes.overview: Changan Automobile's dedicated new energy brand, launched in Australia in late 2024 by leading distributor Inchcape with the head-turning Deepal S07 SUV.

makes.name: Dodge
makes.overview: Historic American marque manufactured in Adelaide by Chrysler Australia (including the iconic Dodge Phoenix), and reintroduced in the 2000s with the Caliber, Nitro, and Journey.

makes.name: Eunos
makes.overview: Mazda's luxury channel in Australia, showcasing boutique dealerships, the world's smallest production V6, and the revolutionary Miller-cycle engine.

makes.name: FSO
makes.overview: Polish manufacturer that imported the rugged, budget-priced FSO Polonez hatchback and commercial utility into Australia.

makes.name: Ferrari
makes.overview: The pinnacle of Prancing Horse exotica in Australia, with privateer motorsport heritage dating to the early 1950s and direct factory subsidiary Ferrari Australasia established in 2013.

makes.name: Fiat
makes.overview: Italian automotive giant that assembled 500, 600, 1100, 1500, and 124 models in Sydney and Melbourne, and thrives today with the iconic modern 500 and Ducato van.

makes.name: Ford Australia
makes.overview: Ford Motor Company of Australia was established in Geelong, Victoria in March 1925 by Canadian-born Hubert French. Beginning with local assembly of the Model T in a disused wool store, Ford went on to become one of Australia's premier automotive manufacturers and innovators. In 1934, Ford Australia young designer Lewis Bandt invented the world's first coupe utility ('ute') in Geelong, creating an automotive category that defined rural and commercial Australia. In September 1960, Ford launched the Falcon, igniting a fierce 56-year rivalry with Holden. Operating major vehicle assembly and stamping complexes at Broadmeadows and engine and casting plants at Geelong, Ford designed, engineered, and manufactured iconic vehicles including the Falcon (XK through FG X), Fairlane, LTD, Territory SUV, and Capri convertible. Although local vehicle manufacturing ceased on 7 October 2016, Ford Australia transformed into Ford's Global Center of Excellence for Ranger and Everest, employing over 2,000 Australian engineers and designers at Campbellfield and the You Yangs Proving Ground.

makes.name: Ford Performance Vehicles (FPV)
makes.overview: Ford Performance Vehicles (FPV) was established in 2002 in Campbellfield, Victoria as a high-performance joint venture between Ford Australia and British racing powerhouse Prodrive, succeeding Tickford Vehicle Engineering (TVE). FPV engineered the most devastating performance Falcons ever created. FPV became renowned for its hand-assembled 'Boss' quad-cam 32-valve 5.4-litre V8s (Boss 290, 302, 315) and the revolutionary turbocharged 'Barra' 4.0-litre twin-cam six in the F6 Typhoon and Tornado (yielding a massive 565Nm of torque). In 2010, FPV introduced the Australian-developed 'Miami' 5.0-litre supercharged V8, crowning its legacy with the limited-edition 2014 FG GT-F 351 (capable of over 400kW on overboost), before operations concluded in late 2014.

makes.name: Foton
makes.overview: Commercial vehicle specialist that pioneered Cummins-powered utes (Tunland) and Aumark light trucks in Australia, evolving into the Tunland V9 hybrid.

makes.name: GWM / Haval
makes.overview: The pioneer of Chinese vehicles in Australia, progressing from the 2009 Great Wall V240 ute to direct factory operations with the GWM Cannon, Haval H6, and Tank 300 off-roaders.

makes.name: Geely
makes.overview: Global automotive giant (owner of Volvo, Polestar, Zeekr, and Lotus) that tested Australian waters in 2011 and officially launched direct factory subsidiary operations in 2024-2025 with the EX5 electric SUV.

makes.name: Genesis
makes.overview: Hyundai Motor Group's standalone luxury brand, operating an agency model with luxury studios in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, and Perth.

makes.name: Giocattolo
makes.overview: Giocattolo Motori Pty Ltd was established in 1986 in Caloundra, Queensland by automotive entrepreneur Paul Halstead and former McLaren Formula 1 engineer Barry Lock. Conceived as Australia's answer to the Ferrari 288 GTO and Porsche 959, the Giocattolo ('toy' in Italian) began with brand-new Alfa Romeo Sprint bodyshells imported from Italy. The front drivetrain was discarded, replaced by a mid-mounted Walkinshaw-fettled Holden Special Vehicles 5.0-litre Group A V8 (220kW/300hp) linked to a bespoke ZF 5-speed transaxle, Kevlar/carbon-fibre composite bodywork, and Brembo racing brakes. Capable of 0-100 km/h in 4.5 seconds and 260 km/h, the Giocattolo was an extraordinary Australian supercar feat. Only 15 production cars were completed before operations ceased in 1989.

makes.name: Hillman / Humber / Sunbeam (Rootes Group)
makes.overview: Rootes Group Australia manufactured Hillmans, Humbers, and Sunbeams at Salmon Street, Port Melbourne, scoring an immortal international victory in the 1968 London to Sydney Marathon with an Australian-built Hillman Hunter.

makes.name: Holden
makes.overview: General Motors-Holden (GM-H) was Australia's definitive domestic automaker and cultural icon. Emerging from an Adelaide saddlery founded by James Alexander Holden in 1856 and later coachbuilding giant Holden's Motor Body Builders (HMBB), Holden partnered with General Motors in 1931 and launched Australia's first mass-produced domestic motor vehicle, the 48-215 (popularly FX), on 29 November 1948. For seven decades, Holden engineered and manufactured vehicles tailored specifically to Australia's vast distances, harsh corrugated roads, and extreme climates at primary assembly complexes in Fishermans Bend and Dandenong (Victoria), Elizabeth and Woodville (South Australia), Pagewood (New South Wales), Acacia Ridge (Queensland), and Mosman Park (Western Australia). From the ubiquitous Kingswood, Monaro, and Torana to the legendary Commodore and luxury Statesman/Caprice, Holden shaped the Australian national identity, dominated Australian motorsport including multiple Bathurst 1000 victories, and exported vehicles across North America, the Middle East, South Africa, and New Zealand before local manufacturing ceased at Elizabeth on 20 October 2017 and the brand retired in 2020.

makes.name: Holden Dealer Team (HDT)
makes.overview: Holden Dealer Team (HDT) Special Vehicles was established in 1980 by nine-time Bathurst champion Peter Brock at 124 Bertie Street, Port Melbourne. When Holden withdrew factory motorsport funding in 1979, Brock purchased the team with financial backing from a coalition of Holden dealers. HDT transformed showroom Commodores into bespoke high-performance road cars with hand-assembled blueprint V8 engines, Bilstein suspension, Scheel sports seats, Momo steering wheels, and wind-tunnel aero bodykits. HDT created Australia's most revered homologation muscle car—the 1985 VK SS Group A 'Blue Meanie'—alongside the VC Brock Commodore, VH Group 3, and VL Group A before Brock's split with Holden in 1987. Today, HDT builds retro heritage editions.

makes.name: Holden Special Vehicles (HSV)
makes.overview: Holden Special Vehicles (HSV) was established in 1987 in Clayton, Victoria as a high-performance joint venture between General Motors-Holden and Scottish racing icon Tom Walkinshaw (Tom Walkinshaw Racing). Born from the ashes of Holden's split with Peter Brock's HDT, HSV elevated Australian muscle cars to world-class engineering standards. Over three decades, HSV developed legendary performance nameplates including the ClubSport, GTS, Senator, and Maloo ute. From the wild aerodynamic composite aero of the 1988 VL Walkinshaw Group A SV to the fire-breathing 375kW 7.0L W427 and the pinnacle 2017 GTSR W1 (474kW supercharged dry-sump LS9), HSV built Australia's most sought-after and collectible high-performance road and track weapons.

makes.name: Honda
makes.overview: Celebrated for Formula 1-derived VTEC engine engineering, high-revving sports icons like the NSX, S2000, and Type R, and family benchmarks like CR-V and Civic.

makes.name: Hummer
makes.overview: General Motors' military-styled 4x4 brand sold through GM Holden dealerships from 2007 to 2010 with the factory RHD Hummer H3.

makes.name: Hyundai
makes.overview: From Alan Bond's initial budget import of the Excel in 1986 to a permanent top-3 market contender renowned for Australian-tuned dynamics, Tucson, Santa Fe, and the i30 N hot hatch.

makes.name: INEOS
makes.overview: Built specifically to fill the void left by the original Land Rover Defender, INEOS chose Melbourne as its Asia-Pacific headquarters to spearhead its rugged 4WD mission in Australia.

makes.name: Infiniti
makes.overview: Nissan's premium performance division sold rear-wheel-drive luxury sedans, coupes, and SUVs through flagship retail centers in Australia.

makes.name: Isuzu / Isuzu UTE
makes.overview: From providing the foundation for the Holden Gemini and Holden Rodeo to dominating Australian ute and SUV sales with the D-MAX and MU-X.

makes.name: JAC Motors
makes.overview: Chinese commercial giant entering Australia's fiercely contested dual-cab ute segment in 2024 with the JAC T9 turbo diesel and electric utilities.

makes.name: JMC
makes.overview: Jiangling Motors Corporation imported the Vigus dual-cab ute into Australia from 2015 to 2018 via JMC Auto Australia.

makes.name: Jaguar
makes.overview: Grace, pace, and space in Australia, distinguished by 1950s local assembly at Enfield NSW, a stunning 1985 Bathurst 1000 victory with the TWR XJ-S, and modern luxury saloons and SUVs.

makes.name: Jeep
makes.overview: The original 4x4 brand, with rich Australian heritage including post-war CKD assembly of Willys and CJ Jeeps in Sydney and Brisbane, through to modern Wrangler, Cherokee, and Grand Cherokee.

makes.name: Kia
makes.overview: From value entry to a top-4 Australian automotive powerhouse, renowned for local suspension tuning, an industry-first 7-year warranty, Carnival, Sportage, and the twin-turbo V6 Stinger.

makes.name: LDV
makes.overview: SAIC-owned commercial and utility marque, imported by Ateco Automotive, famous for the T60 dual-cab ute (and Australia's first electric ute, the eT60), G10 and Deliver 9 commercial vans.

makes.name: Lada
makes.overview: Soviet/Russian automotive manufacturer that captured an Australian cult following with the unbreakable, permanent four-wheel drive Lada Niva.

makes.name: Lamborghini
makes.overview: Sant'Agata's raging bull supercars in Australia, captivating enthusiasts from the Miura and Countach through the V10 Gallardo and Huracán, and Urus super-SUV.

makes.name: Lancia
makes.overview: Pioneering Italian engineering marque beloved by Australian enthusiasts for the Fulvia, Flavia, Beta, and rally-legend Delta Integrale.

makes.name: Land Rover
makes.overview: The backbone of Australian outback exploration, military transport, and luxury off-roading, with extensive local assembly at Enfield and Moorebank NSW including the iconic Australian Army Perentie 4x4 and 6x6.

makes.name: Leapmotor
makes.overview: Innovative EV brand backed by multinational giant Stellantis (Leapmotor International), launching in Australia in late 2024 with the C10 medium SUV and T03 city car.

makes.name: Lexus
makes.overview: Toyota's luxury division launched in Australia in May 1990, redefining premium ownership through obsessive build quality, hybrid technology, and the Lexus Encore service program.

makes.name: Leyland / BMC Australia
makes.overview: The British Motor Corporation (Australia) and later Leyland Australia was a major domestic automotive manufacturer operating from its sprawling, integrated 60-acre manufacturing plant at Victoria Park / Zetland in Sydney, New South Wales. In the 1950s and 1960s, BMC Australia was the third major force in Australian motoring, engineering unique local adaptations like the Morris Major, Austin Freeway, Austin 1800 'Landcrab' and Ute, and the iconic Australian-designed Mini Moke. In the early 1970s, under managing director Peter North, Leyland Australia invested $21 million to take on Holden and Ford directly with a clean-sheet Australian full-size car: the Leyland P76. Designed by Michelotti with an advanced all-alloy 4.4-litre V8, McPherson strut suspension, and a boot capable of swallowing a 44-gallon drum, the P76 won the 1973 Wheels Car of the Year. However, quality issues during early production, component supply strikes, the 1973 oil crisis, and parent company British Leyland's UK collapse forced the closure of Zetland in late 1974, ending one of Australia's most daring manufacturing chapters.

makes.name: Lightburn
makes.overview: Lightburn & Co. was an Adelaide-based manufacturing firm founded by Harold Lightburn, famed across Australia for building concrete mixers, washing machines, and fiberglass powerboats. In 1963, Lightburn made an ambitious leap into automobile manufacturing with the Zeta, a fiberglass-bodied microcar produced in Camden Park, South Australia. Powered by an air-cooled British Villiers 324cc 2-stroke motorcycle engine driving the front wheels, the Zeta featured a motorcycle-style sequential gearbox and no reverse gear—the driver stopped the engine and restarted it running backwards. Lightburn also produced the attractive Zeta Sports roadster and a commercial Zeta Utility before production ceased in 1966 after approximately 400 vehicles.

makes.name: Lotus
makes.overview: Colin Chapman's 'simplify, then add lightness' philosophy in Australia, from classic Elan and Esprit to the Elise, Exige, and bonded aluminium Emira.

makes.name: MG Motor
makes.overview: From classic British sports cars assembled at BMC Zetland Sydney (MGA and MGB) to today's SAIC-owned volume powerhouse dominating Australian light cars and the acclaimed MG4 rear-drive EV.

makes.name: MINI
makes.overview: One of Australia's most revered nameplates, manufactured at BMC Zetland Sydney (yielding unique Australian features, 1966 Bathurst 500 class domination, and the Australian Moke) and reborn globally under BMW.

makes.name: Mahindra
makes.overview: Indian 4x4 powerhouse renowned in regional Australia for the indestructible Pik-Up commercial ute, rugged Scorpio 4WD, and 7-seat XUV700 family SUV.

makes.name: Maserati
makes.overview: The Trident marque of Modena, celebrated in Australia for grand touring elegance, Ferrari-built V8 symphonies, and bespoke Italian luxury.

makes.name: Mazda
makes.overview: Renowned for innovative engineering, rotary-powered motorsport legends, and stylish consumer favourites. Mazda has consistently stood as Australia's second best-selling automotive marque for over two decades.

makes.name: McLaren
makes.overview: Woking's Formula 1-derived supercar manufacturer, delivering carbon-fibre MonoCell architecture, dihedral doors, and twin-turbo performance to Australian roads.

makes.name: Mercedes-Benz
makes.overview: The gold standard of luxury, safety, and performance in Australia, distinguished by historic local CKD assembly in Port Melbourne and world-leading AMG performance sales.

makes.name: Mitsubishi
makes.overview: From manufacturing over 1.1 million cars at Tonsley Park, South Australia to dominating outback tracks with the Pajero and Triton, Mitsubishi is embedded in Australia's automotive fabric.

makes.name: Morgan
makes.overview: Handcrafted traditional British sports cars built with ash wood subframes in Malvern Link, imported to Australia for discerning purists.

makes.name: Nissan
makes.overview: From the Datsun 1600 and local manufacturing at Clayton, Victoria, to the legendary 'Godzilla' Skyline GT-R and indestructible Patrol, Nissan is central to Australian motoring history.

makes.name: OKA Motor Company
makes.overview: OKA Motor Company was established in 1986 in Bibra Lake, Perth, Western Australia to engineer and manufacture an uncompromising, severe-duty all-terrain four-wheel-drive commercial vehicle. Designed to conquer the harshest Australian outback conditions for mining companies, outback tour operators, and emergency services, the OKA featured a massive perimeter steel box-section chassis, heavy-duty Dana 60 front and Dana 70 rear live axles, a bulletproof New Process / Spicer transfer case, and Perkins 4-cylinder (Phaser 110MT) or Cummins 5.9L ISBe turbo-diesel engines. Available across LT, XT, and NT series in single-cab, dual-cab, multicab, bus, and van configurations, the OKA earned legendary status throughout the Kimberley, Pilbara, and Red Centre as an unyielding off-road machine capable of crossing rivers and sand dunes where standard 4WDs perished.

makes.name: Opel
makes.overview: General Motors' German brand had an extensive presence in Australia rebadged as Holdens (Astra, Barina, Vectra, Calibra, Insignia), but operated briefly as an independent marque from 2012 to 2013.

makes.name: Peugeot
makes.overview: Historic French marque immortalized in Australian outback rallying and local CKD assembly of 403, 404, 504, and 505 models at Heidelberg and Clayton, Victoria.

makes.name: Polestar
makes.overview: Born from Volvo's touring car racing team and performance arm, Polestar launched Australia as an early pilot market before establishing an independent pure-electric luxury brand.

makes.name: Pontiac
makes.overview: GM-H manufactured Pontiac Laurentians and Parisiennes in Melbourne, Sydney, and Adelaide, before Australia exported Holden Monaros and Commodores back to America as the Pontiac GTO and G8.

makes.name: Porsche
makes.overview: The pre-eminent German sports car manufacturer, with Australia holding the distinction of being Porsche's very first right-hand-drive market in the world.

makes.name: Proton
makes.overview: Malaysian national carmaker that achieved cult Australian status with the Jumbuck compact coupe utility and Lotus-tuned Satria GTi hot hatch.

makes.name: RAM Trucks
makes.overview: The pioneer of full-size American pickup trucks in Australia, re-engineered and remanufactured to OEM right-hand drive standards by Walkinshaw Automotive in Clayton, Victoria.

makes.name: Rambler / AMC
makes.overview: Manufactured at Port Melbourne by Australian Motor Industries (AMI) from 1960 to 1977, producing right-hand drive Classic, Rebel, Matador, Hornet, and rare Javelin muscle cars.

makes.name: Renault
makes.overview: French innovator that operated an extensive manufacturing plant at Heidelberg, Victoria from 1959 to 1981, and achieved modern acclaim through Renault Sport hot hatches and commercial vans.

makes.name: Rolls-Royce
makes.overview: The quintessential symbol of automotive perfection, handcrafting royal tour cars, viceregal state limousines, and modern Goodwood masterpieces.

makes.name: Rover
makes.overview: Distinguished British carmaker that assembled P5, P6, and SD1 models at Enfield and Zetland NSW, winning 1977 Wheels Car of the Year with the SD1 3500.

makes.name: SEAT
makes.overview: Spanish marque distributed in Australia during the late 1990s by Ateco Automotive, offering Volkswagen-engineered hatchbacks and sedans.

makes.name: Saab
makes.overview: Quirky, aerospace-inspired Swedish carmaker celebrated in Australia for turbocharging leadership, wraparound windscreens, and ignition keys between the front seats.

makes.name: Smart
makes.overview: Daimler's micro-car pioneer, introduced to Australia in 2003 with the City-Coupé, Fortwo, and Roadster, and reborn in 2024 as an all-electric premium compact SUV brand.

makes.name: SsangYong / KGM
makes.overview: Specialists in rugged ladder-frame utes and heavy-duty 4x4 wagons, originally powered by Mercedes-Benz-derived drivetrains and rebranded to KGM in 2024.

makes.name: Studebaker
makes.overview: Manufactured locally at Canada Bay (Sydney) and Motor Producers (Clayton), Studebaker was celebrated for the Lark V8, which served as Australia's first purpose-built high-speed police pursuit vehicle.

makes.name: Subaru
makes.overview: Subaru built a fiercely loyal following in Australia through boxer engines, symmetrical all-wheel drive, outback rally dominance, and rugged crossover utility.

makes.name: Suzuki
makes.overview: Masters of lightweight 4x4s, cheerful hatchbacks, and cult oddities like the Mighty Boy. Celebrated for Jimny, Swift GTi, and Vitara.

makes.name: TVR
makes.overview: Blackpool's outrageous, lightweight fibreglass beasts—no ABS, no traction control, pure thunderous Rover V8 and Speed Six power.

makes.name: Tata Motors
makes.overview: Indian industrial giant that sold the Telcoline ute in the late 1990s and relaunched the Xenon commercial utility in Australia from 2013 to 2017.

makes.name: Tesla
makes.overview: The pioneer and market leader of electric vehicles in Australia, transforming the automotive landscape with the top-selling Model 3 and Model Y and an extensive nationwide Supercharger network.

makes.name: Toyota
makes.overview: Australia's perpetual market leader and automotive titan. Toyota began Australian operations in 1958 with LandCruisers on the Snowy Mountains Scheme and assembled vehicles locally at Port Melbourne and Altona from 1963 to 2017.

makes.name: Triumph
makes.overview: Sporting British marque assembled in Melbourne by Australian Motor Industries (AMI) from 1959 to 1976, celebrated for the 2000/2500 saloons, Dolomite Sprint, and TR sports cars.

makes.name: Vauxhall
makes.overview: General Motors' British division had a foundational role in Australia: Holden built unique Australian bodies for Wyverns, Veloxes, and Crestas, and the Vauxhall Viva HB served as the direct mechanical parent of the legendary Holden Torana.

makes.name: Volkswagen
makes.overview: Volkswagen has been a core pillar of Australian motoring for over seven decades, progressing from local CKD assembly of the Beetle and Kombi at Clayton, Victoria to an expansive European passenger and commercial vehicle line-up.

makes.name: Volvo
makes.overview: Renowned worldwide for safety innovation and in Australia for local assembly of the 140/240 series, Bathurst-winning touring cars, and rapid transition to electrified SUVs.

makes.name: XPENG
makes.overview: High-tech smart EV manufacturer entering Australia in late 2024 with the 800V silicon carbide G6 coupe-SUV, distributed by TrueEV.

makes.name: Yugo
makes.overview: Zastava's Yugoslav city car that claimed the title of Australia's cheapest brand-new car in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

makes.name: ZX Auto
makes.overview: Hebei Zhongxing Automobile sold the GrandTiger dual-cab ute in Australia from 2013 to 2016 via Chinese Automotive Distributors.

makes.name: Zeekr
makes.overview: Geely Holding's premium luxury electric brand, launching in Australia in late 2024 with the Zeekr X compact luxury crossover and Zeekr 009 ultra-luxury electric MPV.

makes.name: Škoda
makes.overview: Czech automotive excellence under the Volkswagen Group, celebrated in Australia for 'Simply Clever' packaging, cavernous wagon space, and value-packed Octavia RS performance.

featured_models.name: Holden Commodore
featured_models.overview: The Holden Commodore was Australia's definitive full-size passenger car, holding the crown as the nation's best-selling car for 15 consecutive years (1996-2010). Spanning 16 distinct series codes across five generations from the original 1978 VB to the billion-dollar Australian-engineered VE/VF Zeta platform and the imported European ZB, the Commodore was the family hauler, police highway patrol interceptor, commercial utility, and Mount Panorama Bathurst racing champion for over four decades.

featured_models.name: Holden Kingswood / Belmont / Premier
featured_models.vehicle_type: Sedan / Wagon / Utility / Panel Van / Cab Chassis
featured_models.overview: The Holden Kingswood was Australia's definitive full-size family car and commercial workhorse from 1968 to 1985. Replacing the HR series with the all-new HK, the Kingswood moniker became an indelible piece of Australian cultural lexicon—celebrated in television ('Kingswood Country'), song, and outback folklore. Encompassing the budget Belmont, mainstream Kingswood, luxury Premier, sporty Monaro-derived options, surf-culture Sandman van/ute, and heavy-duty One Tonner cab-chassis, over 1.5 million examples were produced across HK, HT, HG, HQ, HJ, HX, HZ, and WB series.

featured_models.name: Ford Falcon
featured_models.overview: The Ford Falcon is one of the most storied names in Australian industrial and cultural history. Manufactured continuously at Broadmeadows, Victoria for 56 years (1960-2016) across seven distinct generations and over 3.5 million units, the Falcon fought an epic rivalry with the Holden Commodore. From the pioneering XK and the legendary XY GT-HO Phase III (the fastest 4-door production car in the world) to the Australian-designed XA hardtop, the bestselling XF, the indestructible Intech and Barra DOHC sixes, the high-revving Boss V8s, and the supercharged Sprint series, the Falcon embodied Australian engineering resilience and high performance.

featured_models.name: Holden Astra
featured_models.overview: Spanning 36 years across seven generations, the Holden Astra was Holden's frontline small car. Launched in August 1984 as the LB/LC Astra, it originated as a badge-engineered Nissan Pulsar assembled in Clayton, Victoria. Under the Button Car Plan, the 1987 LD Astra combined Nissan body engineering with Holden's locally manufactured 1.6L and 1.8L Family II engines. In 1996, the Astra was reborn as the TR series, imported from Opel in Europe. The 1998 TS Astra became a massive commercial triumph, winning Wheels Car of the Year and spawning the hot hatch SRi and SRi Turbo (147 kW). The 2004 AH brought dynamic European styling and the 177 kW Astra VXR, followed by the PJ VXR coupe and the final high-tech 2016-2020 BK Astra hatchback (European Car of the Year) before Holden's retirement.

featured_models.name: Holden EJ / EH / HD / HR
featured_models.vehicle_type: Sedan / Station Sedan / Utility / Panel Van
featured_models.overview: The 1962-1968 era represents the golden age of 1960s Holden dominance. The July 1962 EJ introduced clean, modern European-inspired styling, the milestone 1,000,000th Holden produced, and the prestigious Premier luxury model with standard automatic, leather bucket seats, and metallic paint. In August 1963, the legendary EH debuted Holden's all-new, world-class 'Red Motor' inline-six—featuring a 7-bearing crankshaft, hydraulic lifters, and 149ci (2.4L) and 179ci (2.9L) capacities. The EH became Australia's fastest-selling car ever, selling over 250,000 units in 18 months and claiming podium fame at Mount Panorama with the EH S4 Bathurst homologation special. The 1965 HD brought wider passenger accommodations and the twin-carburettor X2 engine, while the April 1966 HR resolved styling with crisp modern lines, front disc brakes, wider track, and the 186S engine with twin-barrel Bendix-Stromberg WW carburettor.

featured_models.name: Camry
featured_models.overview: The Toyota Camry was the cornerstone of Australian automotive manufacturing from 1987 to 2017. Built in Port Melbourne and Altona, it was Australia's favourite mid-size family and fleet sedan for over three decades.

featured_models.name: Corolla
featured_models.overview: The Toyota Corolla is the world's most produced passenger car and an integral part of Australian life. Assembled locally in Victoria for over 30 years (1968-1999), it has provided dependable motoring for generations of Australians.

featured_models.name: Pulsar
featured_models.overview: The Nissan Pulsar is one of Australia's most historic small-car badges. Manufactured locally at Nissan's Clayton plant in Victoria through the 1980s and early 1990s, the Pulsar sired genuine Australian performance legends, from the local 1980s Pulsar Turbo ET to the iconic N14/N15 Pulsar SSS with its high-revving 2.0-litre SR20DE engine and the rally-homologated N14 GTI-R.

featured_models.name: Beetle, Kombi & Country Buggy
featured_models.vehicle_type: Sedan / Convertible / Microbus / Van / Ute / Off-Roader
featured_models.overview: The bedrock of Volkswagen's Australian history. Starting with CKD assembly in Melbourne in 1954, the Type 1 Beetle and Type 2 Kombi progressed to full local manufacture at Clayton, Victoria, achieving over 80% Australian domestic content. Clayton also designed and manufactured the unique Australian Volkswagen Country Buggy (Type 197).

featured_models.name: Golf
featured_models.overview: The benchmark European hatchback in Australia across eight generations. The Golf introduced front-wheel drive hatchback dynamics to Australia, initially assembled locally at Clayton, Victoria, and evolved into Australia's favorite hot hatchback through the legendary Golf GTI and all-wheel-drive Golf R.

featured_models.name: Chrysler Valiant
featured_models.overview: The Chrysler Valiant was the spirited contender of the Australian family car triumvirate alongside the Holden Kingswood and Ford Falcon. Manufactured at Chrysler Australia's sprawling Tonsley Park complex in Adelaide from 1962 to 1981 across 13 series (R, S, AP5, AP6, VC, VE, VF, VG, VH, VJ, VK, CL, CM), the Valiant established an enduring reputation for unmatched horsepower, introducing the 145 hp Slant-6 in 1962, Australia's first family car V8 in 1965, the world-renowned Australian-engineered HEMI-6 in 1970, and pioneering Electronic Lean Burn (ELB) computer management.

featured_models.name: Ford Cortina
featured_models.overview: The Ford Cortina held a distinguished two-decade tenure in Australia, evolving from a nimble British compact into a uniquely Australian six-cylinder muscle sedan. Assembled locally from 1962 (Mk1 and Mk2), the Cortina achieved legendary status when the Bob Jane / Harry Firth Cortina GT500 won the 1965 Armstrong 500 at Mount Panorama, Bathurst. In 1971, Ford Australia undertook a daring local engineering feat with the TC and TD Cortina: modifying the British 'Coke-bottle' body with an elongated front structure to accommodate Ford Australia's heavy 200ci (3.3L) and 250ci (4.1L) Falcon inline-six engines. The European-styled TE (1977) and TF (1980) brought crisp lines, Ghia luxury, and the sporty X-Pack before being succeeded by the Mazda-based Telstar in 1982.

featured_models.name: FPV GT & F6
featured_models.overview: The FPV GT and F6 were Ford Performance Vehicles' crowning high-performance icons. Developed in Campbellfield, Victoria by Ford Australia and Prodrive, this duo formed the greatest domestic performance confrontation in Australian history against HSV. The GT revived Ford's iconic muscle heritage with the quad-cam 32-valve Boss 290 and Boss 315 V8s, before adopting the supercharged 5.0L 'Miami' V8 and culminating in the 2014 GT-F 351 (delivering over 400kW on overboost). Concurrently, the F6 Typhoon transformed Australian performance perceptions with its devastating turbocharged Barra 4.0-litre straight-six, producing up to 565Nm of flat-line torque and supercar acceleration.

featured_models.name: Holden Cruze
featured_models.overview: The Holden Cruze nameplate lived two major chapters in Australia. First launched from 2002 to 2006 as the YG Cruze, it was an innovative subcompact all-wheel-drive crossover co-developed with Suzuki (based on the Ignis) featuring elevated ground clearance and 1.5L power. In 2009, Holden revived the name with the JG Cruze sedan. Most significantly, from March 2011 until October 2016, Holden invested over $1 billion to manufacture the JH Cruze Series II locally on a dedicated assembly line alongside the Commodore at Elizabeth, South Australia. The Australian-built Cruze featured an Australian-designed 5-door hatchback body style, local steering and suspension tuning, high-spec SRi and SRi-V turbo models (1.4L and 1.6L 132 kW turbos), and an efficient 2.0L Turbo Diesel. Over 125,000 Cruzes were built at Elizabeth.

featured_models.name: Holden Sandman
featured_models.overview: The Holden Sandman is the undisputed emblem of 1970s Australian youth and beach culture. Introduced in January 1974 on the HQ series (option package XX7 / XU3), the Sandman transformed humble commercial panel vans and utilities into vibrant, psychedelic recreational machines. Featuring bold side stripes, Monaro GTS sports dashboard with tachometer, GTS steering wheel, slotted steel rally wheels, twin bucket seats, and standard or optional 253ci and 308ci Red V8 power, the Sandman became a pop-culture legend closely tied to surfing, drive-in cinemas, and Australian freedom. The Sandman package carried through the HQ, HJ, HX, and HZ series until 1980, with authentic surviving examples now among Australia's most fiercely sought-after collector cars.

featured_models.name: HSV ClubSport & GTS
featured_models.overview: The HSV ClubSport and GTS formed the beating heart of Holden Special Vehicles from 1990 to 2017. Developed at HSV's performance facility in Clayton, Victoria, the ClubSport was HSV's top-selling performance sedan, while the GTS served as the technological flagship. From the original VN ClubSport and VP GTS (with 4-bolt mains and IRS) to the stroker 5.7L V8s, the 300kW Callaway C4B in the VT/VX, the E-Series Magnetic Ride Control, the supercharged 430kW LSA in GEN-F, and the crowning 2017 GTSR W1 (powered by the dry-sump 474kW Corvette ZR1 LS9 supercharged V8), this model line represents the pinnacle of Australian rear-wheel-drive muscle car engineering.

featured_models.name: Crown
featured_models.overview: The Toyota Crown established Toyota's reputation for engineering refinement and reliability in Australia. Built locally from CKD packs by Australian Motor Industries (AMI) in Port Melbourne from 1967 to 1979, the Crown offered six-cylinder prestige, luxurious appointments, and long-legged durability across five distinct Australian generations.

featured_models.name: Corvette & Silverado
featured_models.overview: The modern pillars of General Motors in Australia under GM Specialty Vehicles (GMSV). The eighth-generation C8 Corvette arrived as the world's first factory right-hand drive Corvette directly from the Bowling Green assembly line, offering mid-engine supercar performance and the spine-tingling 500kW flat-plane crank Z06. Alongside it, the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and 2500HD are remanufactured to RHD in Melbourne by Walkinshaw Automotive Group, delivering up to 1,322Nm of Duramax V8 torque and heavy towing capability.

featured_models.name: Chrysler Centura
featured_models.overview: The Chrysler Centura (KB and KC series) was Chrysler Australia's audacious weapon to conquer the mid-size family car market dominated by the Holden Torana and Ford Cortina. Assembled at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, Chrysler imported European Simca 180 bodyshells from France and undertook radical local re-engineering to shoehorn Chrysler Australia's mighty Australian-cast 3.5L (Hemi 215) and 4.0L (Hemi 245) pushrod straight-six engines, alongside a French 2.0L Simca 4-cylinder. With 123 kW (165 hp) and 319 Nm of torque propelling a compact 1,200 kg body, the Hemi 245 Centura was an astonishing sleeper muscle sedan, sprinting from 0-100 km/h in under 9 seconds and completing the standing quarter-mile in 16.5 seconds. 19,770 units were produced across the KB (1975-1977) and updated KC (1977-1978).

featured_models.name: Chrysler / Mitsubishi Sigma
featured_models.overview: The Chrysler Sigma—later renamed Mitsubishi Sigma after Mitsubishi acquired Chrysler Australia in 1980—was the undisputed king of Australia's four-cylinder family car market across the late 1970s and 1980s. Manufactured at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, the Sigma (GE, GH, GJ, GK, GN) dethroned traditional six-cylinder cars by offering expansive interior space, European-influenced styling, four-wheel coil spring suspension, and revolutionary 'Silent Shaft' counter-rotating balance shafts in its Australian-cast Astron 1.85L, 2.0L, and 2.6L engines. The GH series introduced the legendary limited-edition Sigma Turbo in 1981 (Australia's first locally built turbocharged production car), while the 1982 GJ series spawned the celebrated Peter Wherrett Special. Over 300,000 Sigmas were built in Adelaide before making way for the Magna.

featured_models.name: Ford F-Series (F-100 / F-250 / F-350 / F-150)
featured_models.overview: The Ford F-Series is an enduring pillar of Australian outback, farming, and heavy towing history. Locally assembled in Australia across multiple decades in Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland, Australian F-100s, F-250s, and F-350s were specifically tailored for harsh Aussie work, utilizing local 250ci Falcon straight-sixes, 300ci big sixes, and Geelong-cast 302ci and 351ci Cleveland V8s. In 2001, Ford Australia officially returned to the heavy-duty market with the mighty RN-series F-250 and F-350, powered by the thunderous 7.3L Navistar Power Stroke Turbo Diesel V8 (175 kW / 684 Nm), creating a cult legend among caravan haulers. In 2023, Ford Australia officially launched the Next-Gen F-150 in Australia, remanufactured to OEM right-hand drive in Mickleham, Victoria featuring the 298 kW 3.5L EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 and 4.5-tonne towing capacity.

featured_models.name: Ford Mustang
featured_models.overview: The Ford Mustang has a storied heritage in Australia stretching back six decades. In 1965, Ford Australia officially imported and converted 400 iconic 1965-1966 notchback Mustangs to right-hand drive at Homebush, NSW, while touring car legend Norm Beechey campaigned a 1965 Mustang to Australia's first Australian Touring Car Championship win for an American V8. In 2001, Ford Tickford Experience (FTE) in Campbellfield, Victoria undertook a heroic $4 million engineering program to convert 250 SVT Mustang Cobras featuring independent rear suspension and 240 kW 4.6L DOHC 32V modular V8s. In late 2015, Ford delivered the first global factory right-hand drive FM Mustang to Australia, creating unprecedented multi-year customer waiting lists. The FM/FN generations and all-new 2024+ S650 generation (featuring the 362 kW 5.0L Gen-4 Coyote V8 and 373 kW Dark Horse) made Mustang Australia's best-selling sports car for seven consecutive years.

featured_models.name: Ford Territory
featured_models.overview: The Ford Territory was the first and only sports utility vehicle (SUV) designed, engineered, and manufactured in Australia. Developed under the code-name 'E265' at a cost of $500 million, the Territory debuted in April 2004 and won the prestigious 2004 Wheels Car of the Year award. Available in 5- and 7-seat configurations, in rear-wheel drive and permanent all-wheel drive, the Territory combined car-like handling, Virtual Pivot Control front suspension, and generous interior packaging, spanning SX, SY, and SZ series with Barra I6, Barra Turbo, and 2.7L V6 turbo-diesel engines.

featured_models.name: Holden Adventra & Crewman
featured_models.vehicle_type: All-Wheel-Drive Cross Wagon / Dual-Cab Utility / Cab Chassis
featured_models.overview: Developed during Holden's multi-million dollar engineering expansion under the VY/VZ Commodore program, the Adventra and Crewman represented audacious Australian engineering innovations. The 2003 Crewman was Australia's first locally designed and manufactured monocoque dual-cab utility, seating five adults on an extended 3,200 mm wheelbase with a heavy-duty leaf-sprung live rear axle capable of carrying up to a tonne. The Adventra was Holden's crossover all-wheel-drive sport wagon, boasting an Australian-engineered 'Cross-Trac' permanent AWD system (62% rear, 38% front torque split with automatic brake-traction management) and raised ground clearance. Holden combined the two concepts to create the monstrous Crewman Cross 8 and Cross 6, alongside V8 SS performance dual-cabs.

featured_models.name: Holden FE / FC / FB / EK
featured_models.vehicle_type: Sedan / Station Sedan / Utility / Panel Van
featured_models.overview: The second and third generation post-war Holdens represented major leaps forward in Australian automotive engineering and design. Launched in July 1956, the FE introduced a completely modern, longer, lower body with wrap-around windscreen, 12-volt electrical architecture, recirculating ball steering, and Holden's very first factory station wagon—marketed as the 'Station Sedan'. The May 1958 FC refined the formula with an egg-crate grille and became the first car in Australian history to sell over 100,000 units in a calendar year. In January 1960, the FB adopted American fin-tail styling and a larger 138ci Grey motor, followed in May 1961 by the EK, which brought the historic introduction of the 3-speed Hydra-Matic automatic transmission to Holden. Across all four series, over 740,000 vehicles were built.

featured_models.name: Holden Torana
featured_models.overview: The Holden Torana (derived from an Aboriginal word meaning 'to fly') is one of Australian motorsport's greatest legends. Starting in 1967 as a modified Vauxhall Viva four-cylinder compact (HB), the Torana evolved into a giant-killing six-cylinder weapon in the LC and LJ series, highlighted by Peter Brock's rainy 1972 Bathurst 500 victory in the triple-carburettor LJ GTR XU-1. The LH and LX generations made Australian automotive history as the only car platform engineered to accommodate 4-, 6-, and 8-cylinder engines, culminating in the Bathurst-dominating SL/R 5000 and A9X option pack.

featured_models.name: Morris Major / Austin Freeway & Wolseley 24/80
featured_models.overview: The Morris Major and Austin Freeway family was BMC Australia's dedicated endeavor to engineer vehicles specifically for Australian motoring conditions at the Victoria Park plant in Zetland, Sydney. Commencing in 1958 as the Morris Major (and sibling Austin Lancer), it adapted the Wolseley 1500 body with increased ground clearance, reinforced suspension, and BMC's 1.5L B-Series four. In 1962, BMC Australia achieved an extraordinary domestic engineering feat: by extending the nose structure and casting two extra cylinders onto the 1622cc B-Series block, they created Australia's first locally designed mass-market inline-six: the 2433cc 'Blue Streak' six. Fitted to the Austin Freeway and the luxury Wolseley 24/80 (featuring genuine burr walnut dashboard and leather seats), the 6-cylinder Freeway competed directly with the Holden and Falcon, offering 59 kW, outback suspension, and optional Borg-Warner 35 automatic transmission.

featured_models.name: Magna
featured_models.overview: The Mitsubishi Magna was an Australian manufacturing triumph, designed specifically for Australian conditions by widening the Japanese Galant by 66mm. Produced at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, it won two Wheels Car of the Year awards (1985, 1996) and culminated in the 180kW Magna Ralliart and revolutionary Magna AWD.

featured_models.name: 240 & 850 Series
featured_models.overview: The twin legends that transformed Volvo's reputation in Australia. The 240 Series was assembled locally at Clayton, Victoria, setting world safety standards and winning the 1986 Australian Touring Car Championship as the 'Flying Brick'. Its successor, the 850 Series, introduced front-wheel drive transverse 5-cylinder performance, celebrated by the limited-edition 850 T-5R and the 850 Super Tourers raced by Peter Brock and Jim Richards.

featured_models.name: Chrysler Valiant Charger
featured_models.overview: The Chrysler Valiant Charger is one of the most charismatic muscle cars in Australian history. Launched in August 1971 with the memorable 'Hey Charger!' television advertising campaign, the Charger was built on a shortened 105-inch wheelbase with stunning fastback proportions, winning the 1971 Wheels Car of the Year award. Immortalized by the legendary Bathurst homologation specials—the E38 (280 bhp) and the triple-Weber E49 'Six Pack' (302 bhp)—the Charger was the fastest-accelerating Australian production car for over a decade, holding the standing quarter-mile record at 14.4 seconds.

featured_models.name: Dodge Phoenix
featured_models.overview: The Dodge Phoenix was Chrysler Australia's grand American luxury flagship from 1960 to 1973. Conceived to compete head-on with the Ford Galaxie and Chevrolet Impala/Bel Air in the prestige government, executive, and pastoralist market, the Phoenix was assembled in Adelaide from North American CKD packs, using Dodge Dart/Polara, Plymouth Fury, and Chrysler bodies married to bespoke factory right-hand drive Plymouth dashboards. Spanning the early finned PD/RD series through to the majestic 'fuselage'-bodied models of 1969-1973, every Phoenix was powered by burly American Chrysler V8 engines—predominantly the 318ci (5.2L) 'Poly' and 'LA' small-block V8s, and the optional 383ci (6.3L) 'B-block' Big Block V8 in the opulent Phoenix 400 Hardtop. Sumptuously appointed with Torqueflite 3-speed automatic transmissions, power steering, push-button radios, and deep plush interiors, the Phoenix was the undisputed car of choice for Australian politicians, judges, and graziers.

featured_models.name: Ford Capri
featured_models.overview: The Ford Capri represents two bold chapters of Australian automotive innovation. In May 1969, Ford Australia began assembling the sleek Mk1 Capri sports coupe at Homebush, NSW, offering the 1600cc Kent and the potent 3.0-litre 'Essex' V6 in the revered Capri GT 3000 (101 kW / 136 bhp), instantly creating an Australian street and track favorite. In 1989, Ford Australia embarked on Project SA30: designing and manufacturing a dedicated front-wheel-drive 2+2 roadster convertible in Campbellfield, Victoria. Styled by Ghia in Turin and utilizing Mazda 323 mechanicals, the Australian-built Capri (SA, SB, SC, SE) was exported in huge numbers to North America as the Mercury Capri. It produced the blistering turbocharged Capri XR2 and the rare Australian Tickford-tuned Capri Clubsprint Turbo.

featured_models.name: Ford Escort
featured_models.overview: The Ford Escort was Ford Australia's frontline small car and grassroots rally champion throughout the 1970s. Manufactured at Ford's Homebush plant in Sydney, the Australian Mk1 (1970-1975) featured the classic 'dogbone' front grille, Kent Crossflow engines (1.1L, 1.3L, and 1.6L GT), and the legendary imported Twin Cam and RS1600. In 1975, the Australian Mk2 debuted with a squarer aerodynamic profile. Ford Australia equipped the Mk2 with the lively 1.6L Kent and the potent 2.0L OHC Pinto engine, culminating in the iconic Escort RS2000 featuring a polyurethane droop-snoot front nose, four-spoke alloy wheels, Scheel sports bucket seats, and rally-bred handling.

featured_models.name: Ford Laser
featured_models.overview: The Ford Laser was one of Australia's most beloved small cars, dominating private sales and motoring awards across the 1980s and 1990s. Born from Ford's global partnership with Mazda (sharing the 323 platform), the Laser was manufactured at Ford's Homebush assembly plant in Sydney with distinct styling penned by Ford Australia's design studio. The Laser spawned the iconic 'TX3' badge—an Australian performance sensation that progressed from the twin-carb KA/KB Sport to the ferocious KC/KE and KF/KH TX3 Turbo 4WD, packing a 1.6L/1.8L turbocharged DOHC engine, full-time four-wheel drive, and digital instruments. Sourcing shifted to Japan in 1994 with the imported KJ, KL, and KQ series before the model was succeeded by the Focus.

featured_models.name: Holden Monaro
featured_models.overview: The Holden Monaro is Australia's most revered two-door muscle car and grand tourer. Introduced in July 1968 with the HK series, the pillarless hardtop coupe captured national imagination by winning the 1968 Bathurst 500 on debut with Bruce McPhee and Barry Mulholland in a GTS 327, followed by Colin Bond's win in the 1969 HT GTS 350. Resurrected thirty-three years later following a sensational reception as the 'Coupe 22' concept at the 1998 Sydney Motor Show, the modern V2 and VZ Monaro CV8 captivated enthusiasts globally and was exported to North America as the Pontiac GTO and the UK as the Vauxhall Monaro.

featured_models.name: Defender
featured_models.overview: The immortal off-road master of the Australian bush and Australian Defence Force. Built and adapted locally with unique Australian military specifications (Project Perentie 4x4 and 6x6 with Isuzu 4BD1 3.9L engines), live-axle County 110s, and re-imagined for the 21st century as the ultra-capable, luxury L663 Defender.

featured_models.name: Austin 1800 / Utility (Landcrab)
featured_models.overview: The Austin 1800 (BMC project ADO17, affectionately nicknamed the 'Landcrab' for its broad track and tenacious roadholding) was manufactured in Australia by BMC and later Leyland Australia at the Victoria Park assembly complex in Zetland, Sydney. Featuring Alec Issigonis's revolutionary transverse engine front-wheel-drive layout, Hydrolastic interconnected fluid suspension, and an astonishingly spacious passenger cabin with 70% of car length devoted to passengers, the 1800 won Wheels Car of the Year in 1965. Australia made two world-exclusive contributions to the model: Australian engineers re-engineered the shell with elevated ground clearance and sump protection for outback endurance (proven by an astonishing 2nd place in the gruelling 1968 London-to-Sydney Marathon); and in 1968, Leyland Australia designed and manufactured the world's only Austin 1800 Utility ('Landcrab Ute'), combining front-wheel drive, a completely flat load bed, and Hydrolastic self-levelling suspension that kept the ute flat regardless of cargo weight! Over 56,000 Austin 1800s were built in Sydney.

featured_models.name: Classic Mini / Cooper / Moke
featured_models.overview: The full story of the Mini in Australia: manufactured in Sydney at BMC Zetland (with Australian-developed wind-up windows and quarter-vents), immortalized by outright victory in the 1966 Bathurst 500, transformed into the Australian-engineered Californian Moke, and reborn as the modern BMW MINI Cooper and John Cooper Works.

The Mitsubishi 380 was the final passenger car designed, engineered, and manufactured by Mitsubishi Motors Australia at its Tonsley Park plant in Adelaide. Backed by a $600-million investment and over 2.4 million kilometres of Australian testing, the 380 was powered by a punchy 3.8-litre 6G75 V6 with 175kW and 343Nm, praised by critics for its exceptionally stiff body structure and European-grade chassis dynamics.

featured_models.name: Skyline
featured_models.overview: The Nissan Skyline represents a crowning achievement in Australian motoring. Locally built at Clayton, Victoria in R31 guise with the RB30E engine, it also dominated Bathurst as the twin-turbo R32 GT-R 'Godzilla', ending the V8 monopoly and reshaping Australian motorsport history.

The legendary French workhorses assembled in Melbourne for almost two decades. Revered across Australia for soaking up horrific outback corrugations with long-travel independent suspension, victorious in the 1970 Ampol Trial, and winning 1970 Wheels Car of the Year.

featured_models.name: RAM 1500
featured_models.overview: The full-size pickup that rewrote the Australian light commercial market. Re-engineered and remanufactured from left-hand drive to right-hand drive by Walkinshaw Automotive in Clayton, Victoria. Delivers 4.5-tonne towing, legendary 5.7L HEMI V8 rumble, expansive crew-cab luxury, and the 523kW supercharged TRX halo.

featured_models.name: Aurion
featured_models.overview: The Toyota Aurion was an Australian-manufactured large front-wheel-drive sedan engineered to compete directly against the Holden Commodore and Ford Falcon. Powered exclusively by the 200kW 3.5-litre 2GR-FE V6 and built at Altona, Victoria, it also sired the legendary Eaton TVS supercharged 241kW TRD Aurion.

featured_models.name: Bolwell Nagari (Mk VIII)
featured_models.overview: The Bolwell Nagari (Mk VIII) was Australia's premier bespoke production sports car, built by Campbell and Graeme Bolwell in Mordialloc, Melbourne. Featuring an ultra-rigid Y-shaped steel backbone chassis, breathtaking fiberglass coachwork, and Ford 302ci/351ci Windsor and Cleveland V8 engines, the Nagari weighed just 1,040 kg and accelerated from 0-100 km/h in 5.8 seconds, outpacing contemporary European exotics. A total of 127 units (100 coupes and 27 convertibles) were built.

featured_models.name: Ford Fairlane & LTD
featured_models.overview: The Ford Fairlane and LTD was Australia's definitive long-wheelbase luxury prestige sedan. Spanning four decades and eleven model series from the 1967 ZA to the 2007 BF Mk II, the Fairlane dominated Australian corporate, hire-car, and government limousine fleets. In 1973, Ford introduced the ultra-exclusive LTD (P5) riding on a limousine-class 121-inch wheelbase with concealed headlamps and standard 351 Cleveland V8. The Fairlane and LTD offered effortless V8 cruising, cavernous rear legroom, and refined Australian engineering.

featured_models.name: Goggomobil Dart
featured_models.overview: The Goggomobil Dart is Australia's most famous and beloved micro-sports car. Conceived and designed by Sydney automotive pioneer Bill Buckle to bypass steep tariffs on imported fully assembled cars, the Dart combined German Hans Glas rolling chassis components with an ultra-lightweight, doorless aerodynamic fiberglass roadster body molded in Brookvale, Sydney. Standing just 1.1 meters tall and weighing only 345 kg, the Dart became an Australian cultural icon, celebrated for its playful styling and immortalized in Australian television advertisements.

featured_models.name: Holden Statesman / Caprice
featured_models.overview: The Holden Statesman and Caprice was Australia's presidential luxury flagship for nearly five decades. Conceived to challenge the Ford Fairlane and LTD, the Statesman rode on an extended 114-inch to 118-inch wheelbase providing unmatched rear legroom. Serving as official transport for Australian prime ministers, diplomats, business executives, and luxury hire car fleets, the Statesman and Caprice evolved from the ornate HQ-WB models to the modern IRS-equipped VQ-WL series and the billion-dollar Zeta-platform WM and WN. Exported globally as the Chevrolet Caprice, Buick Park Avenue, and US Police Pursuit Vehicle (PPV).

featured_models.name: Leyland P76
featured_models.overview: The Leyland P76 was Australia's most daring automotive gamble. Developed under project leader Peter North at BMC/Leyland's Zetland plant in Sydney to break the Holden-Ford-Chrysler monopoly, the P76 was styled by Italian master Giovanni Michelotti. It boasted world-class engineering: an all-aluminium 4.4-litre V8 derived from Rover weighing less than rivals' iron sixes, standard front power disc brakes, MacPherson strut front suspension, side-impact door bars, and a boot famously demonstrated by swallowing an entire 44-gallon drum. The P76 won the 1973 Wheels Car of the Year and conquered the 1974 World Cup Rally across the Sahara before factory closure cut short its life.

featured_models.name: Brabham BT62 / BT62R
featured_models.overview: The Brabham BT62 and BT62R was an ultra-exclusive mid-engine hypercar manufactured in Adelaide, South Australia by Brabham Automotive, led by Le Mans winner David Brabham. Developed without turbochargers or hybrid battery weight, the BT62 featured a high-tensile tubular steel chassis with integrated carbon-kevlar monocoque safety cell, carbon-fibre body panels, and a mid-mounted naturally aspirated 5.4-litre modular V8 revving to 8,200 rpm and developing 522 kW (700 hp) and 667 Nm. Generating 1,200 kg of aerodynamic downforce with a dry weight of only 972 kg, the BT62 shattered closed-cockpit lap records at Mount Panorama Bathurst (1m 58.69s).

featured_models.name: Giocattolo Group B
featured_models.overview: The Giocattolo Group B was an authentic Australian mid-engine supercar engineered by entrepreneur Paul Halstead and former McLaren Formula One designer Barry Lock in Caloundra, Queensland. Starting with imported Alfa Romeo Sprint bodyshells, Halstead and Lock discarded the front-drive powertrain and installed a mid-mounted Walkinshaw-fettled Holden Special Vehicles 5.0L Group A V8 (220kW/300hp), a bespoke ZF 5DS-25/2 five-speed transaxle, Kevlar/carbon-fibre composite bodywork, and Brembo racing brakes. Accelerating from 0-100 km/h in 4.5 seconds with a top speed of 260 km/h, only 15 production cars were built before funding ended in 1989.

featured_models.name: HDT VK SS Group A ('Blue Meanie')
featured_models.overview: The HDT VK SS Group A, universally affectionately known as the 'Blue Meanie', is the most revered homologation muscle car in Australian touring car racing history. Built by Peter Brock's Holden Dealer Team Special Vehicles at 124 Bertie Street, Port Melbourne in 1985, the Group A was created to homologate the Commodore under international FIA Group A racing regulations. All 500 cars were painted in striking Formula Blue, featuring a de-stroked 4.9-litre (4987cc) V8 with Crane cam and roller rockers, M21 4-speed manual gearbox, Scheel velour bucket seats, and distinctive white 16-inch Aero alloy wheels.

featured_models.name: Holden 48-215 (FX)
featured_models.overview: The Holden 48-215 (retrospectively referred to as the 'FX') was Australia's first mass-produced domestic motor vehicle, famously unveiled on 29 November 1948 by Prime Minister Ben Chifley with the words: 'She's a beauty!'. Developed under GM Project 2000, it combined American interior room and robust unibody construction with European operating economy, tailored specifically for Australia's harsh corrugated roads. In January 1951, the 50-2106 Coupe Utility was launched, defining the iconic Australian 'ute', followed in July 1953 by the 48-215-257 Business Sedan for taxi operators. Over 120,402 examples were produced.

featured_models.name: Holden FJ
featured_models.overview: Launched in October 1953, the Holden FJ is Australia's most recognized cultural automotive icon of the 1950s. Featuring an assertive horizontal chrome tooth grille, redesigned torpedo rear styling, and the introduction of the luxurious 'Special' sedan badge with two-tone leather options, the FJ captured 50% of Australian new car registrations. In December 1953, the iconic FJ Panel Van was introduced, creating the quintessential Aussie tradesman vehicle. The FJ was also Holden's first exported model, shipped to New Zealand in 1954. Total production reached 169,969 units.

featured_models.name: Holden Gemini
featured_models.overview: The Holden Gemini was Australia's best-selling four-cylinder car of the 1970s and early 1980s. Developed from GM's global T-car platform (shared with the Opel Kadett C, Isuzu Bellett Gemini, and Chevrolet Chevette), the Gemini won the prestigious 1975 Wheels Car of the Year award on debut. Over 226,000 units were produced across TX, TC, TD, TE, TF, and TG rear-wheel-drive series before transitioning to the front-wheel-drive RB series.

featured_models.name: Lightburn Zeta Sedan
featured_models.overview: The Lightburn Zeta was South Australia's unique fiberglass microcar, manufactured by industrial equipment firm Lightburn & Co. in Camden Park, Adelaide. Powered by a British Villiers 324cc two-stroke twin-cylinder motorcycle engine driving the front wheels through a 4-speed sequential dog transaxle without reverse (the engine was stopped and restarted in reverse rotation), the Zeta was impervious to corrosion and designed to provide economical suburban motoring.

featured_models.name: OKA 4x4 (LT, XT, NT)
featured_models.overview: The OKA 4x4 was an uncompromising, severe-duty all-terrain four-wheel-drive commercial truck manufactured in Bibra Lake, Perth, Western Australia. Engineered specifically to endure the most punishing outback corrugations, mine sites, and desert terrain across Australia, the OKA featured an indestructible heavy-duty perimeter box-section chassis, Dana 60 front and Dana 70 rear live drive axles, New Process transfer case, and Perkins/Cummins turbo-diesel power across LT, XT, and NT generations.

featured_models.name: Z-Car (Fairlady Z)
featured_models.overview: The Datsun and Nissan Z-Car is one of the most celebrated sports car dynasties in Australian automotive history. From the breathtaking 1970 Datsun 240Z that conquered Jaguar E-Types and MGs on price and performance to the twin-turbo technology tour-de-force 300ZX, the pure rear-drive naturally aspirated 350Z and 370Z, and the modern 298kW twin-turbo RZ34 Z Coupe, the Z represents affordable, exhilarating grand touring sports car excellence.

featured_models.name: Liberty & Outback
featured_models.overview: The Subaru Liberty (Legacy globally) and Outback revolutionized Australian family and touring motoring. Spanning seven generations, the Liberty delivered rally-bred AWD performance with the BC RS Turbo, twin-turbo B4, and 2003 Wheels Car of the Year winning BL/BP GT Spec.B, while the lifted Outback pioneered the crossover wagon genre in 1996 and evolved into Australia's ultimate all-road adventure tourer.

featured_models.name: Celica
featured_models.overview: The Toyota Celica was Australia's definitive Japanese sports coupe for 34 years across seven generations. From the Mustang-inspired TA22 and RA28 liftbacks of the 1970s to the championship-winning turbo all-wheel-drive GT-Four rally homologation specials and high-revving 2ZZ-GE VVTL-i ZR, the Celica defined stylish sports performance.

featured_models.name: LandCruiser
featured_models.overview: The LandCruiser is the undisputed King of the Australian Outback. First brought to Australia in 1958 for the Snowy Mountains Scheme, it has conquered the country's most unforgiving deserts, pastoral stations, and mines for nearly seven decades.

featured_models.name: 626 / Mazda6
featured_models.overview: The Mazda 626 and its successor the Mazda6 served as Australia's benchmark mid-size Japanese passenger car for 45 years. From the 1983 Wheels Car of the Year winning front-wheel drive 626 GC to the ferocious 190kW Mazda6 MPS turbocharged all-wheel-drive performance hero, it balanced executive styling with dynamic driver engagement.

featured_models.name: Forester
featured_models.overview: The Subaru Forester is an Australian automotive legend that helped pioneer the compact all-wheel-drive crossover genre in 1997. Blending permanent Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive, high ground clearance, commanding estate-car visibility, and turbocharged WRX engines in GT and XT badges, it earned an intensely loyal following among Australian families, campers, and rural motorists.

featured_models.name: HiLux
featured_models.overview: The Toyota HiLux is an Australian cultural icon and the country's best-selling vehicle outright from 2016 through 2022. Renowned for near-indestructible durability, it serves on construction sites, farms, mining operations, and outback tracks nationwide.

featured_models.name: Civic & Civic Type R
featured_models.overview: The Honda Civic is an undisputed benchmark of global and Australian automotive engineering. Spanning eleven generations over more than 50 years, the Civic conquered Australian hearts during the 1970s oil crisis with its revolutionary CVCC clean-burn engine, democratized Formula 1-derived VTEC variable valve timing in the 1990s VTi-R, and evolved into front-wheel-drive circuit royalty with the ferocious Civic Type R.

featured_models.name: HiAce
featured_models.overview: The Toyota HiAce is the unquestioned titan of Australian commercial vans and passenger shuttle transport. Across more than half a century, its cab-over and semi-bonnet configurations have kept Australian tradespeople, couriers, airport shuttles, and tourism fleets moving with renowned reliability and outstanding resale value.

featured_models.name: LandCruiser Prado
featured_models.overview: The Toyota LandCruiser Prado is Australia's perennial favorite family and long-distance outback touring 4WD. Bridging the gap between the mid-size RAV4 and heavy-duty LandCruiser wagon, the Prado delivers genuine off-road capability, dual long-range fuel tanks, up to seven seats, and legendary durability.

featured_models.name: A3, S3 & RS3
featured_models.overview: The pioneer of the premium compact segment in Australia. Spanning four generations (8L, 8P, 8V, and 8Y), the A3 introduced luxury hatchback packaging and quattro all-wheel drive, reaching high-performance zeniths with the S3 quattro and the spine-tingling 2.5-litre turbocharged inline-5 Audi RS3 producing 294kW.

featured_models.name: 5 Series & M5
featured_models.overview: The definitive executive express in Australia across eight generations. The 5 Series established BMW's benchmark rear-wheel-drive chassis dynamics, silky inline-sixes, and thunderous V8s, culminating in the peerless BMW M5 from the high-revving S38, naturally aspirated V8 S62, screaming V10 S85, to the twin-turbo V8 M xDrive M5 Competition.

featured_models.name: Mazda3
featured_models.overview: The Mazda3 is one of Australia's most beloved passenger cars, achieving the rare feat of becoming the country's outright best-selling vehicle in 2011 and 2012. Known for sporty dynamics, sharp KODO design, and high-performance MPS editions.

featured_models.name: MX-5
featured_models.overview: The Mazda MX-5 is the world's best-selling two-seater sports car and an icon of pure driving pleasure in Australia. Embodying the philosophy of 'Jinba Ittai' (horse and rider as one), the MX-5 revived the classic British roadster concept with Japanese reliability, near-perfect 50:50 weight distribution, and rear-wheel-drive purity.

featured_models.name: E-Class
featured_models.overview: The heartbeat of Mercedes-Benz in Australia. From the virtually indestructible W114/W115 and W123 that conquered outback roads and taxi fleets, through the peerless Bruno Sacco W124, to supercharged V8 E55 AMG and twin-turbo 450kW E63 S AMG monsters.

featured_models.name: Outlander
featured_models.overview: The Mitsubishi Outlander is one of Australia's most enduring family SUVs and a pioneer of plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) technology. Known for offering 7-seat practicality in a medium SUV footprint, robust all-wheel drive systems derived from the Lancer Evolution, and exceptional value, the Outlander is a mainstay on Australian roads.

featured_models.name: Navara
featured_models.overview: The Nissan Navara is one of Australia's premier dual-cab and commercial utes. Spanning four generations, from the durable D21 and indestructible D22 workhorses to the powerhouse 550Nm V6 turbodiesel D40 and coil-sprung D23 with locally engineered Premcar Warrior editions, the Navara has served on Australian building sites, farms, and off-road expeditions for nearly four decades.

featured_models.name: Patrol
featured_models.overview: The Nissan Patrol is an Australian outback giant. In 1962, the G60 Patrol made history as the first motor vehicle to cross the Simpson Desert. Across MQ, GQ, GU, and the V8-powered Y62, it has matched the LandCruiser blow for blow across Australia's harshest terrain.

The definitive rear-engine sports car. Australia boasts one of the most historic ties to Porsche in the world: Melbourne businessman Norman Hamilton secured the Australian concession in 1951, importing two 356s that represented the first right-hand drive Porsches ever made. Since the 911's local launch in 1965, it has defined sports car perfection through air-cooled and water-cooled eras, culminating in legendary Turbo, GT3, and GT3 RS icons.

featured_models.name: 3 Series
featured_models.overview: The benchmark executive sports sedan in Australia across seven distinct generations: E21, E30, E36, E46, E90, F30, and G20. Revered for near-perfect 50:50 weight distribution, rear-wheel drive chassis balance, silky inline-six engines, and iconic M3 motorsport heroes.

featured_models.name: X5
featured_models.overview: The vehicle that redefined the luxury SUV category in Australia. Originating in 2000 as the world's first true Sports Activity Vehicle (SAV) with monocoque construction and car-like handling, the BMW X5 has dominated Australian luxury SUV sales across four generations.

featured_models.name: Holden Rodeo
featured_models.vehicle_type: Ute / Cab Chassis / Space Cab / Crew Cab 4x2 & 4x4
featured_models.overview: For nearly three decades from 1980 to 2008, the Holden Rodeo was one of Australia's most trusted commercial workhorses and outback touring utilities. Engineered by Isuzu Motors and sold through Holden dealerships across Australia, the Rodeo spanned the tough KB series (1980-1988), the long-running TF series (1988-2003, famous for its bulletproof 2.8L 4JB1-T turbo-diesel and 3.2L V6), and the redesigned RA series (2003-2008). The Rodeo pioneered crew-cab four-wheel-drive dual-cab versatility in Australia, proving equally adept on cattle stations, mining sites, and suburban driveways before being renamed Colorado in 2008.

featured_models.name: X-Trail
featured_models.overview: The Nissan X-Trail is an Australian compact and medium SUV institution. Famous for combining utilitarian practicality—such as wipe-clean waterproof cargo floors, cooled cup holders, and multi-tier drawers—with genuine soft-road capability via Nissan's All-Mode 4x4, it remains one of Australia's most consistently popular family crossovers.

featured_models.name: WRX
featured_models.overview: The Subaru Impreza WRX and WRX STI democratized supercar-baiting all-wheel-drive turbocharged performance in Australia in 1994. Backed by Possum Bourne's seven consecutive Australian Rally Championships, the WRX is an indelible part of modern Australian car culture.

featured_models.name: Supra
featured_models.overview: The Toyota Supra is a halo sports grand tourer with an indelible legacy in Australian motorsport and enthusiast culture. From early Celica Supra models through the twin-turbo 2JZ-GTE JZA80 supercar killer to the modern B58-powered GR Supra, it represents Toyota's front-engine rear-drive inline-six performance pinnacle.

featured_models.name: Echo / Yaris / GR Yaris
featured_models.overview: Toyota's light car family in Australia spans from the quirky, spacious Echo through three generations of Yaris hatchbacks and sedans to the hyper-capable GR Yaris Rallye AWD homologation special. Combining exceptional reliability, hybrid fuel efficiency, and World Rally Championship engineering, it is a giant of small-car motoring.

featured_models.name: Ford Focus
featured_models.overview: The Ford Focus replaced the Laser in 2002 and immediately established itself as Australia's benchmark dynamic driver's car in the compact segment thanks to its revolutionary 'Control Blade' multi-link rear suspension. Across four generations (LR, LT/LV, LW/LZ, and SA), the Focus earned critical acclaim. For Australian car enthusiasts, the Focus name was cemented by legendary performance flagships: the 2.0L high-revving LR ST170 (127 kW), the five-cylinder turbo LT/LV XR5 Turbo (166 kW 2.5L Volvo turbo) and limited-edition 224 kW Focus RS, the sensational 257 kW drift-mode AWD LZ Focus RS, and the nimble SA Focus ST.

featured_models.name: Holden Barina
featured_models.overview: For over 33 years across six generations, the Holden Barina was Australia's quintessential light car. Introduced in February 1985 as the MB Barina (a badge-engineered Suzuki Cultus made unforgettable by poet Pam Ayres' commercial: 'Beep beep, Barina!'), the model transitioned through the ML, MF, and MH series. In 1994, Holden pivoted to GM Europe with the SB Barina (Opel Corsa B), creating an Australian youth lifestyle phenomenon that produced the cult Barina GSi (1.6L 16V twin-cam). The 2001 XC Barina won Wheels Car of the Year 2001. Sourcing moved to GM Daewoo in 2005 with the value-focused TK, while the final 2011-2018 TM Barina featured GM's global Gamma II platform, culminating in the sporty Barina RS powered by a 103 kW 1.4L Turbo engine.

featured_models.name: i30
featured_models.overview: The Hyundai i30 is the vehicle that transformed Australian perceptions of the brand from budget-oriented to class-leading. Winner of the 2007 Wheels Car of the Year, it has been an Australian small car benchmark and gave rise to the sensational Albert Biermann-developed i30 N hot hatch.

featured_models.name: XJ & XJ-S
featured_models.vehicle_type: Large Luxury Sedan / Grand Tourer Coupe
featured_models.overview: The apex of British automotive grandeur and motorsport glory. Sir William Lyons' XJ6 was declared the finest riding saloon in the world upon its Australian release, while the V12 XJ12 and XJ-S grand tourer achieved immortality when Tom Walkinshaw Racing's Jaguar XJS V12 conquered Mount Panorama to win the 1985 Bathurst 1000. Evolved through supercharged XJR flagships to the bonded-aluminium X350 and avant-garde X351.

featured_models.name: CX-5
featured_models.overview: The Mazda CX-5 is one of Australia's all-time most popular SUVs, holding the title of best-selling SUV in the country outright for multiple consecutive years.
